title: The weights, and what they cost to move
kicker: 09 · The weights, and what they cost to move

scenes.name: from a parameter count to a byte count
scenes.visual: Dark canvas. Top band, centre: an equation that builds term by term, 'memory = parameter count × bytes per parameter', with 'parameter count' in blue, 'memory' and 'bytes per parameter' in coral, the operators in white. Middle band: the worked line, each piece landing under its own term: '70 billion parameters', '× 2 bytes', '= 140 GB, in 16-bit precision'. A small grey side note sits to the right of the worked line. Bottom right, arriving only in the last beat: a small G P U package miniature, an amber square labelled 'chip' with an empty coral-outlined container beside it labelled 'memory beside the chip'. The equation and worked line persist until the last beat, when the result swells into a solid coral block and slides into that container. The idea the motion makes visible: a count of weights becomes an amount of bytes, and those bytes are a physical thing that has to sit somewhere.

beats.say: Earlier you counted every weight in the model. But a memory chip doesn't store weights. It stores bytes. So first, a conversion you will use constantly. Memory equals the parameter count, times the bytes per parameter.
beats.show: Top-left, the small blue ledger card from the previous chapter, '70.6 B parameters', appears and fades. The equation builds left to right on the spoken words: 'memory' (coral) on 'memory equals', '=' draws on, 'parameter count' (blue) on 'parameter count', '×' on 'times', 'bytes per parameter' (coral) on 'bytes per parameter'.

beats.say: Seventy billion parameters. Each is stored in sixteen bits, which is two bytes. Seventy billion times two is a hundred and forty billion bytes. A hundred and forty gigabytes, in sixteen-bit precision.
beats.show: Under 'parameter count', a blue counter runs from 0 to '70,000,000,000' on 'seventy billion'. Under 'bytes per parameter', a strip of 16 small bit cells appears on 'sixteen bits', splits into two groups of 8 each tagged 'byte', then collapses into a tile '× 2 bytes'. On 'a hundred and forty gigabytes', the coral result '= 140 GB, in 16-bit precision' lands under 'memory'.

beats.say: With the exact count from earlier, seventy point six billion, it comes to a hundred and forty-one. Close enough. The round hundred and forty is the number we'll carry.
beats.show: Grey side note to the right of the worked line: '70.6 B × 2 = 141.2 GB', then '≈ 140 GB' beneath it. The note dims to 40% and stays.

beats.say: Notice the formula has two knobs. A bigger model means more bytes. Or give each weight fewer bytes: store it in one byte instead of two, and the same model is seventy gigabytes. That second knob gets a later video of its own.
beats.show: Two small dial icons appear, one under 'parameter count', one under 'bytes per parameter'. On 'one byte instead of two', the second dial turns from '2' to '1'; the coral result morphs from '140 GB' to '70 GB' while a thin coral bar under it halves in length. Grey tag 'a later video'. The dial turns back to '2' and the result returns to '140 GB'.

beats.say: That hundred and forty gigabytes is the entire model. It sits in one pool of memory beside the chip, off the chip itself. It does not change between requests. It is the model.
beats.show: The equation and side note fade. The coral '140 GB' result swells into a solid coral block and slides down-right into the empty container beside the amber 'chip' square. Tags appear on the spoken phrases: 'the entire model', 'off the chip', 'does not change between requests'. Last line, white, centred under the package: 'It is the model.'

scenes.name: three places, three speeds
scenes.visual: Header across the top: 'Reading 140 GB from each place'. Three rows down the left third, each an icon and a label: a hard-drive icon 'From a disk'; a memory-module icon 'From the memory beside the chip (H100)'; a processor icon 'From the chip's own memory'. The right two thirds hold one shared linear time axis, 0 to 20 seconds across about 1,500 px, ticks every 5 s, faint grey along the bottom, tagged 'same scale'. Row 1 gets a full-width coral bar; row 2 a coral bar about 3 px wide, truly to scale, shown under a magnifier; row 3 gets no bar at all. A stopwatch icon sits top-right. All three rows persist; the disk row leaves in the last beat. The idea: three tiers, wildly different speeds, and only the middle one both fits the model and is fast.

beats.say: Why there, beside the chip? You met three places the file can sit. Now time them side by side, doing the same job each time: reading all hundred and forty gigabytes.
beats.show: Header draws on. The three rows' icons and labels fade in top to bottom on 'three places'. The faint time axis draws along the bottom with the tag 'same scale'. The stopwatch appears top-right at '0 s'.

beats.say: From a disk, at roughly seven gigabytes a second for a fast drive, it takes about twenty seconds. Twenty thousand milliseconds.
beats.show: Row 1's coral bar grows from 0 to the 20 s mark over about two seconds of screen time, with a small grey tag 'time-lapse'; the stopwatch runs to '20 s'. At the bar's end: grey '≈ 7 GB/s', white 'about 20,000 ms'.

beats.say: From the memory beside the chip, at the H one hundred's three point three five terabytes per second, it takes about forty-two milliseconds.
beats.show: Row 2's bar appears in a blink: a coral sliver about 3 px wide on the same axis. Labels: grey '3.35 TB/s', white 'about 42 ms'. A magnifier circle pops over the sliver and shows it enlarged, so the viewer can see it is really there.

beats.say: Twenty thousand divided by forty-two is roughly five hundred. That's why, on the same scale, the second bar is barely a sliver.
beats.show: A bracket joins rows 1 and 2 at the right with amber '20,000 ÷ 42 ≈ 480×', then white 'roughly 500×' beneath it. The magnifier shrinks away.

beats.say: Make that concrete. Read the weights off a disk for every token, and a three-hundred-token answer takes about a hundred minutes. From the memory beside the chip, about twelve and a half seconds. So the model is loaded once, and stays there.
beats.show: Two small timer cards slide in at the right, each beside its row: row 1 'a 300-token answer: ≈ 100 min' in coral, row 2 'a 300-token answer: ≈ 12.5 s' in teal. On 'loaded once', the cards fade and a teal arrow labelled 'load once' sweeps from the disk icon down into the memory icon.

beats.say: The disk numbers are approximate, and vary widely by hardware. The gap between the tiers does not.
beats.show: Grey tag under row 1: 'disk figures approximate, vary by hardware'. White tag between rows 1 and 2: 'the gap does not'.

beats.say: The third row is not slow. It is impossible. The chip keeps a few hundred kilobytes in each of its small working areas, about a tenth of a gigabyte in all. A hundred and forty gigabytes is more than a thousand times too big. It does not fit.
beats.show: Row 3: no bar. A tiny blue box at the axis origin labelled '≈ 0.1 GB, whole chip', with a smaller grey tag 'a few hundred KB per working area'. A coral block labelled '140 GB' slides along the row toward the box and stops dead against it, unable to enter. White label 'it does not fit', coral '> 1,000× too big'.

beats.say: So the disk row explains why start-up is slow, and why nobody streams weights from storage. After the load, it never appears again.
beats.show: Row 1 turns grey and slides off the left edge, trailing the tag 'start-up only'. Row 2 brightens and moves to centre: the memory beside the chip is where everything happens from here on.

scenes.name: inside the package
scenes.visual: The G P U package illustration seen from above, centred and large. A blue rounded slab labelled 'one package'. In its centre an amber rectangle labelled 'GPU die', the processing chip. Around it five coral HBM stacks, three down the left side and two down the right, with a faint dashed outline of a sixth, unused site on the right (the real H100 package has six sites with five in use). Mid-scene the camera dives into one stack and tilts it into a side cross-section: eight thin coral layers, each a 'die' (label shown on the top three, plus a '× 8' tag), with thin vertical lines running down through all of them. Then the camera pulls back and rotates the whole package to a side view: a long blue slab along the bottom, a coral stack on the left and the amber die on the right, a small gap between them marked 'millimetres', and a dense fan of hair-thin lines across the slab joining them. Colour by meaning: amber for the processing chip, coral for memory and for the bytes on the wires, blue for the package and the slab.

beats.say: So what is that memory beside the chip, physically? You know its name, high bandwidth memory, H B M. Here is a G P U package seen from above. In the middle sits the processing chip, the slab of silicon holding those thousands of workers.
beats.show: The blue slab draws on, label 'one package'. Title tag top-left: 'HBM = high bandwidth memory'. On 'the processing chip', the amber rectangle fades in at the centre, label 'GPU die'.

beats.say: A single flat slab of silicon like that is called a die. Around it stand the towers of memory you heard about earlier, the stacks. The H one hundred has five.
beats.show: On 'called a die', the 'GPU die' label pulses. Five coral stacks pop in one at a time around the die, three left and two right, with a small counter stepping 1 to 5. A faint dashed sixth outline on the right carries the grey tag 'unused site'. One stack gets the label 'HBM stack'.

beats.say: Look inside one stack. It is a pile of memory dies, each thinner than a sheet of paper, bonded one on top of another. Thousands of tiny vertical connections run straight down through them all.
beats.show: The camera dives into the front-left stack and tilts it into a side cross-section: eight thin coral layers build upward one by one, the top three labelled 'die', tag '× 8'. On 'vertical connections', thin lines draw downward through all eight layers, tag 'connections through the silicon'.

beats.say: On the H one hundred, each stack is eight dies tall and holds sixteen gigabytes. Five stacks of sixteen is eighty gigabytes, the capacity on the spec sheet. Building upward packs more memory into the little floor space beside the chip.
beats.show: Beside the cross-section: '8 dies → 16 GB'. The camera pulls back to the top view; the five stacks light in turn while a counter steps '16, 32, 48, 64, 80 GB'. A small spec-sheet card slides in, 'Memory capacity: 80 GB', and ticks. Tag: 'build up, not out'.

beats.say: Now turn the package on its side. The stacks and the processing chip are bonded side by side onto one shared slab of silicon, millimetres apart. Across that gap runs the bus, one thousand and twenty-four wires from every stack.
beats.show: The camera rotates to the side view: blue shared slab along the bottom, a coral stack on the left, the amber die on the right. A dimension arrow 'millimetres' spans the gap. A dense fan of hair-thin lines draws across the slab between them, tag '1,024 wires per stack'.

beats.say: Five stacks make five thousand one hundred and twenty wires, all carrying bits at the same moment. A very wide parallel bus. Each stack delivers about six hundred and seventy gigabytes a second. Together, three point three five terabytes per second.
beats.show: The view widens to show five fans of wires side by side, one per stack; counter '5 × 1,024 = 5,120 wires'. Coral particles flow along every wire at once. Five small flow counters '≈ 670 GB/s' slide together and sum into one larger coral counter '3.35 TB/s'.

scenes.name: close and wide, small and expensive
scenes.visual: Split screen, divided by a faint grey vertical line. Left half: the H100 side view from the previous scene, shrunk: a coral stack and the amber die on a blue slab, a 'millimetres' gap, a dense fan of hair-thin coral lines. Right half: a laptop circuit board seen from the side: an amber processor and a coral memory module several centimetres apart on a dark grey board, joined by a sparse band of thicker lines, with a 'centimetres' dimension arrow. A one-line header across the top changes with each beat; at most two tags per side. Midway the right half clears for a capacity comparison drawn as bars to scale. Then the split dissolves and the full package returns in side view, all five stacks and the die, for the trip the bytes make on every pass. The idea: the bandwidth comes from placement, placement has a price, and close is still not on.

beats.say: Here is what the name really means. It is not faster memory chips. You saw earlier that each of these wires runs no faster than a laptop's, about five or six billion bits a second.
beats.show: The split builds. Identical grey per-wire tags on both sides: left '≈ 5.2 Gbit/s per wire', right '≈ 6 Gbit/s per wire'. Header: 'not faster chips'.

beats.say: The difference is placement. A laptop's memory sits centimetres from its processor, joined by about a hundred and twenty-eight wires. H B M sits as close as physically possible, millimetres away, joined by five thousand one hundred and twenty. Forty times as many.
beats.show: Dimension arrows draw on: 'centimetres' on the right, 'millimetres' on the left. Wire counters: right '128', left '5,120'. Amber between the halves: '5,120 ÷ 128 = 40×'. Header: 'close and wide'.

beats.say: And wide needs short. To fit thousands of wires side by side, each has to be microscopically thin. A wire that thin only carries a clean signal over millimetres. Stretch it to centimetres, and high and low blur together.
beats.show: Header: 'wide needs short'. The left fan zooms in: crisp square coral pulses run along hair-thin lines. On 'stretch it', one thin wire stretches out to the length of the laptop's connection; its square pulse smears into a soft, blurred wave, grey tag 'high and low blur'. It snaps back.

beats.say: That's why the memory can't simply be moved further away and made bigger. The name describes a placement, not a technology. Close and wide.
beats.show: A grey hand cursor drags the left stack away from the die; the wire fan stretches, frays and turns grey. The stack snaps back into place and the wires turn coral again. Header: 'a placement, not a technology'.

beats.say: The price is that it is small and expensive. Every stack has to fit in that little floor space beside the chip, and bonding dies this precisely is a costly way to build memory.
beats.show: Header: 'small and expensive'. A price-tag icon appears beside the left stack. The laptop board on the right fades out, leaving the right half empty.

beats.say: Eighty gigabytes is less than our one model. That's why the H one hundred was a what-if earlier: a model this size is really spread across two chips or more. Here, keep the simple picture, one chip reading the whole model.
beats.show: Right half, bars to scale: a coral bar '80 GB, one H100' and above it a longer coral outline '140 GB, the model' overhanging by 60 GB; grey tag 'two chips or more, a later video'. On 'keep the simple picture', the bars dim.

beats.say: And close is still not on. Every forward pass, one trip through all eighty layers to make one token, reads all hundred and forty gigabytes out of H B M, across that bus, into the arithmetic units.
beats.show: The split dissolves; the full package returns in side view, five stacks and the die on the slab. Coral particles stream from every stack across the bus into the amber die, where each flashes amber and vanishes. A coral counter under the bus runs from 0 to '140 GB'; tag 'one forward pass'.

beats.say: Every single time. Strictly, almost all: on the way in, the embedding table gives up only a handful of rows, as you saw earlier. That spares about two gigabytes, so the round number stands.
beats.show: The counter resets and runs to '140 GB' again, labelled 'pass 2', then 'pass 3', faster each time. Small grey note along the bottom: 'embedding table: a few rows read, ≈ 2 GB spared, ≈ 139 GB per pass'.

beats.say: High bandwidth memory is close, and it is wide. But it is still off the compute die. That trip, across a few millimetres, is what everything from here on is about.
beats.show: The camera pushes in on the gap between the nearest stack and the die until the gap fills the centre of the frame and glows coral. Final line, white, centred: 'close and wide, but still off the die'.

scenes.name: read, never written
scenes.visual: Centre: one coral block labelled '140 GB of weights', with a small lock icon on its corner. Header: 'Nothing about the weights changes while the service runs'. Left and right of the block, a user icon each with a speech bubble. A bottom band arrives midway: a horizontal bus line from a coral 'HBM' block at the left to an amber 'chip' block at the right, with a token counter above it; right of the chip, a small blue box '≈ 0.1 GB on chip' used when the layers stream through. End state: two large arrows from the centre pointing in opposite directions, teal to the left and coral to the right. The idea: one unchanging fact, with two consequences that point opposite ways.

beats.say: One more fact about these bytes, and it matters as much as their size. Memory can be read, which copies numbers out, or written, which changes them. In training, these weights were written trillions of times. While the service runs, they are only ever read.
beats.show: Header draws on; the coral block fades in centre. On 'read', a teal arrow copies a small tile out of the block, label 'read: copy out'. On 'written', a pencil icon hovers over the block, label 'write: change'; on 'only ever read', the pencil is crossed out in grey and the lock icon clicks shut. Small inset bottom-left: grey 'training: trillions of writes', white 'serving: reads only'.

beats.say: Two different users, two different questions. One asks about tomorrow's weather. The other wants help with some code. The same numbers do the work for both, and are left exactly as they were.
beats.show: A user icon slides in on the left with bubble 'weather tomorrow?'; another slides in on the right with bubble 'fix my code'. Coral copy-streams flow from the block to both users at once. The block does not change; tag under it: 'the same 140 GB, for every request from every user'.

beats.say: The one thing that does change as people talk is the running record the server keeps of each conversation. That comes back later. The weights themselves never change.
beats.show: Beside each user a small blue strip grows a little, label 'running record, per conversation', grey tag 'later'. The coral block stays exactly as it was; the lock glints.

beats.say: That's why one copy in memory can serve everybody. A thousand users, each with a private copy, would need a hundred and forty terabytes of this small, expensive memory. Instead, one copy serves them all.
beats.show: Behind the block, ghost copies multiply into a large faint grid while a counter reads '1,000 × 140 GB = 140 TB'. On 'one copy serves them all', the grid collapses back into the single block. Teal tag: 'one copy serves everyone'.

beats.say: It's also what makes batching possible. When several users' tokens are ready at the same moment, one read of the weights can do the work for all of them. That idea comes back later.
beats.show: Blue token pills from both users ride together on one coral flow leaving the block. Teal tag: 'batching: one read, many users'; small grey 'later'.

beats.say: Now the other side of the same fact. The reading is pure overhead. The same bytes cross the same bus for every token. On an H one hundred, flat out, that's about twenty-four times a second.
beats.show: The users fade. The bottom band builds: coral 'HBM' block at left, the bus line, amber 'chip' at right, a token counter above. Each tick of the counter sends an identical coral packet '140 GB' across the bus. Amber note: '3.35 TB/s ÷ 140 GB ≈ 24 per second'.

beats.say: A five-hundred-token answer reads the same hundred and forty gigabytes five hundred times. That's the seventy terabytes you met earlier, every pass identical to the last.
beats.show: The token counter accelerates to '500'; a coral running total climbs to '70 TB'. Each packet that crosses gets a faint grey stamp 'identical'.

beats.say: Why not keep the weights on the chip after one read? Because the chip holds about a tenth of a gigabyte. Even one layer's weights, about one point seven gigabytes, are more than ten times too big.
beats.show: Right of the chip, the small blue box '≈ 0.1 GB on chip' appears. A coral tile 'one layer ≈ 1.7 GB' tries to drop into it and overflows it many times over; amber '1.7 ÷ 0.12 ≈ 14×'.

beats.say: So the slices stream through and are dropped. By the time layer eighty is done, layer one is long gone, and the next token starts again from layer one. Nothing is learned by reading the weights, and nothing is saved by having read them before.
beats.show: Small coral tiles labelled 'layer 1', 'layer 2', and on to 'layer 80' stream through the box, each pushing the previous one out. On 'the next token', the counter ticks and 'layer 1' is fetched across the bus again. Tag: 'nothing learned, nothing saved'.

beats.say: Two consequences, pointing opposite ways. One copy can serve everyone. And yet the same bytes must be re-read, every single time.
beats.show: Everything clears to two large arrows from the centre: teal pointing left, 'one copy serves everyone'; coral pointing right, 'the same bytes, re-read every token'.

beats.say: So the toll for each pass is fixed: a hundred and forty gigabytes. What can change is how much useful work one pass gets done. And that differs enormously between reading a prompt in and writing an answer out.
beats.show: The coral arrow condenses into a fixed tag '140 GB per pass: fixed'. The teal arrow turns into a question mark, 'work per pass?'. Two faint grey labels fade in below: 'reading the prompt in', 'writing the answer out'.
